title: The Borel quotient of a semisimple-rank-one reductive group is a curve
statement: Let $F$ be an algebraically closed field [def-weil-field, def-weil-algebraic-closure]. All groups are affine $F$-group schemes [def-sc-group-scheme] of finite type [def-weil-finite-type-morphism], and all subgroups are closed subgroup schemes [def-sc-group-scheme-subgroup]. Let $G$ be reductive and $T\subseteq G$ a maximal torus, as in [def-sfb-reductive-torus-centralizer-terminology]. Let $R(G)$ be the largest smooth connected solvable normal subgroup, where solvable means that successive scheme-theoretic commutator subgroup schemes eventually become trivial. Assume every maximal torus of the represented fppf quotient $G/R(G)$ [lem-sfb-affine-normal-quotient-geometry] has dimension one [def-kun-topological-krull-dimension]. For every Borel subgroup $B\supseteq T$ [def-sfb-borel-subgroup-scheme], the scheme $G/B$ representing the fppf sheaf quotient of right cosets [lem-sfb-homogeneous-orbit-quotient-geometry] has Krull dimension one. No characteristic restriction is imposed.

proof.text: Take the smooth connected projective flag scheme $Y=\mathcal B(G)$ of [lem-sfb-general-borel-flag-variety], with the point $b_B$ whose scheme stabilizer is $B$. By [lem-sfb-smooth-group-orbit-geometry] its orbit $O$ is locally closed, and by [lem-sfb-homogeneous-orbit-quotient-geometry] the orbit with reduced structure is $G/B$. The transitivity in the flag statement shows that $O$ contains every $F$-point of $Y$. Every closed point of $Y$ has residue field $F$ by [lem-weil-pbc-closed-point-residue-field-base]. Thus $O$ contains all closed points. By [lem-sc-lft-over-field-jacobson-space] these are dense in $Y$, so the locally closed $O$ is open; its closed complement has no closed points and hence is empty by the same density statement. The scheme $Y$ is reduced by [sbc-lem-smooth-geometrically-reduced]. A reduced locally closed subscheme with dense open support in a reduced scheme is that open subscheme: its radical defining ideal has zero radical and is zero. Consequently $O=Y$ as schemes. This identifies $G/B$ with $Y$, equivariantly for $G$. In particular we can use the nonempty, connected, proper finite-type scheme $Y$ to compute the dimension of the quotient in the statement.

source.place: Theorem 20.16 (b) implies (c), printed p.413; identification of the Borel variety with G/B, with the orbit argument expanded.

proof.text: Apply [lem-sfb-rank-one-opposite-borel-intersection] to the given $G,T,R(G)$. Its hypotheses are exactly the reductivity and quotient-rank hypothesis of this item. Its first conclusion gives exactly two Borel subgroups containing $T$. By the bijection and fixed-point clause of [lem-sfb-general-borel-flag-variety], these give exactly two scheme-theoretically $T$-fixed $F$-points of $Y$, and these points are distinct. Only the two-Borel clause is used, not the stronger intersection assertion.

source.place: Theorem 20.16 (a) implies (b), printed p.412, and (b) implies (c), printed p.413.

proof.text: Apply [lem-sfb-proper-homogeneous-torus-fixed-bound] with $H=B$, $S=T$, and $X=G/B\simeq Y$. All its hypotheses hold: reductivity supplies smoothness and connectedness of $G$, a Borel is closed, a torus is split over the algebraically closed field, and properness was obtained in step 1. For $d=\dim Y$, the bound supplies $d+1$ distinct fixed points, whereas step 2 supplies exactly two. Therefore $d\leq1$.

source.place: Theorem 20.16 (b) implies (c), printed p.413, using Corollary 20.12, printed p.411.

proof.text: If $d\leq0$, [lem-weil-pbc-finite-type-dim-zero-artinian] makes the nonempty connected finite-type scheme $Y$ a finite discrete topological space. A nonempty connected discrete space has exactly one point $y$. It is closed, so [lem-weil-pbc-closed-point-residue-field-base] identifies its residue field with $F$. Every $F$-point with image $y$ factors through $\operatorname{Spec}\kappa(y)$, and its residue-field map must be the unique inverse of this identification; hence there is only one $F$-point of $Y$. This contradicts the two distinct points in step 2. Thus $d>0$, and together with step 3 this gives $d=1$. The equivariant quotient identification of step 1 gives $\dim(G/B)=1$ for the arbitrary given $B\supseteq T$.

Step 1 identifies Y=B(G) with G/B: transitivity puts every F-point in the orbit, closed points are F-points and dense, so the orbit is open with empty complement, Y is reduced, and the identification is equivariant. Step 2 uses only the two-Borel clause of rank-one-opposite-borel-intersection, whose hypotheses are word for word the item's; the flag bijection turns these into two distinct fixed points. Step 3 applies the new Cor 20.12 node with H=B, S=T, whose hypotheses I checked, giving d<=1. Step 4 excludes d=0 with dim-zero-artinian: a single point has a single F-point, which contradicts step 2. This fills the gap Milne leaves. The new node is a faithful general statement of Cor 20.12 (any H, any torus, no reductivity), not a clause of the item. I tested r=0, G=H, G_m on P^n (sharp bound), SL2/PGL2/GL2 and a nonsmooth H.
